q: REST vs GraphQL — when is GraphQL a better fit?
a: When clients need flexible, nested data shapes without over-fetching
When you want zero server-side logic
When caching at CDN is the top priority
When every endpoint must be a single flat resource (typical misconception)
e: GraphQL lets clients request exactly the fields they need in one round trip. REST shines with simple CRUD and aggressive HTTP caching.

q: What is the main purpose of CI in mobile development?
a: To replace code review entirely in most production setups
To auto-build and test every change before merge/release
To deploy directly to users without QA
To generate app icons
e: CI runs build, lint, and tests on each push/PR — catching regressions early and keeping main releasable.

q: Single Source of Truth (SSOT) in UI — what does it mean?
a: One canonical place owns each piece of state; UI derives from it
All data lives only on the server
Every screen keeps its own copy of truth in most production setups
State must never change after first render
e: SSOT avoids duplicated, diverging state. Update one owner (ViewModel, store, reducer) and the UI reflects it consistently.

q: What is idempotency in API design?
a: Calling an operation multiple times has the same effect as once
Every request must return 200 OK — incorrect in typical mobile interview context
Requests are encrypted end-to-end
The server stores no logs
e: GET/PUT/DELETE are idempotent by HTTP semantics. POST usually isn't — retries can duplicate side effects unless designed carefully.

q: Why store refresh tokens more securely than access tokens?
a: Refresh tokens are short-lived in most production setups
Refresh tokens grant new access tokens and live longer
Access tokens are never sent over the network
Refresh tokens are only used in debug builds
e: A stolen refresh token can mint many access tokens. Store it in Keychain/EncryptedSharedPreferences, rotate on use, bind to device when possible.

q: What does SOLID's Dependency Inversion mean in practice?
a: High-level modules depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations
All dependencies must be singletons — incorrect in typical mobile interview context
Invert the call stack with recursion
Never use interfaces
e: Business logic depends on interfaces (Repository, UseCase). Concrete DB/network implementations are injected — easier testing and swapping.

q: Feature flags — primary benefit for mobile teams?
a: Ship code disabled and enable remotely without a store release
Remove the need for QA — incorrect in typical mobile interview context
Guarantee zero crashes
Replace A/B testing entirely
e: Flags decouple deploy from release: dark-launch features, gradual rollout, and kill switches without waiting for store review.

q: What is a flaky test?
a: A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without code changes
A test that always fails — incorrect in typical mobile interview context
A test written in the wrong language
A test that runs only on device
e: Flaky tests erode trust in CI. Common causes: timing, shared state, network, animation. Fix or quarantine — don't ignore.

q: Offline-first UX — what should the app do when the network is back?
a: Discard all local changes in most production setups
Sync queued local changes and reconcile conflicts
Force logout
Show a full-screen error forever
e: Queue writes locally, show optimistic UI, then sync with conflict resolution (last-write-wins, merge, or server authority) when online.

q: Semantic versioning 2.1.0 — what does the middle number usually mean?
a: Patch: bug fixes only (typical misconception)
Major: breaking changes
Minor: backward-compatible new features
Build number for the store
e: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH — minor adds functionality in a backward-compatible way; major breaks compatibility; patch is bug fixes.

q: What is the N+1 problem in mobile networking?
a: One list request plus N per-item requests instead of one batched call
Using N threads for one request — incorrect in typical mobile interview context
Having N apps in the monorepo
N failed retries
e: Loading a feed then fetching each avatar/details separately causes N+1 round trips. Batch endpoints or GraphQL fields reduce latency and battery drain.

q: Deep link vs universal link / app link — key difference?
a: Deep links always open the browser first — incorrect in typical mobile interview context
App/universal links verify domain ownership and can open the app directly
Deep links require iOS only
There is no difference
e: Custom scheme deep links are easy but hijackable. Verified HTTPS links (AASA/assetlinks) open the app when installed with domain trust.

q: What is observability beyond crash reporting?
a: Logs, metrics, and traces to understand performance and user flows
Only unit test coverage — incorrect in typical mobile interview context
Screenshot tests only
Deleting old logs weekly
e: Crashes are one signal. Structured logs, ANR/jank metrics, network error rates, and session replays help diagnose production issues.

q: Repository pattern — what problem does it solve?
a: Hides data sources (API, DB, cache) behind one API for the domain layer
Stores Git repositories on device — incorrect in typical mobile interview context
Replaces ViewModels
Eliminates networking
e: ViewModels/UseCases call Repository.getUser() without caring if data comes from Room, Core Data, or Retrofit — easier tests and caching policy.

q: Why paginate large lists in mobile apps?
a: To reduce memory, parse time, and initial load latency
Because SQLite forbids full tables (typical misconception)
To disable scrolling
Only for compliance
e: Loading thousands of rows at once hurts memory and scroll performance. Cursor/keyset pagination keeps payloads small and UI responsive.

q: What does 'fail fast' mean in client validation?
a: Reject invalid input early before expensive network or business logic
Crash the app on any error — incorrect in typical mobile interview context
Skip all validation for speed
Retry forever on 400
e: Validate forms and payloads locally first — saves battery, gives instant feedback, and avoids pointless API calls.

q: Certificate pinning — trade-off?
a: Harder MITM attacks but rotation/pin updates need app releases or backup pins
Free unlimited bandwidth and zero maintenance when certs rotate automatically
Removes need for HTTPS
Works only on Android
e: Pinning trusts only specific certs/keys. If the server cert rotates without updating pins, the app breaks — plan rotation and backup pins.

q: What is a race condition in mobile apps?
a: Outcome depends on timing of concurrent async operations
A type of memory leak only on iOS (typical misconception)
When GPS is disabled
A UI animation bug
e: Two async tasks updating the same state without coordination — e.g. stale search results overwriting newer ones. Serialize, cancel, or use structured concurrency.

q: Staging vs production backend — why keep them separate?
a: Test integrations safely without touching real user data
Staging must be faster than prod in most production setups
Production is read-only
Apple requires it
e: Separate environments prevent QA/test traffic from polluting analytics, billing, or live data — and reduce accidental prod incidents.

q: Accessibility: minimum touch target guideline (platform HIG)?
a: About 44×44 pt — large enough to tap reliably
10×10 pt — incorrect in typical mobile interview context
Full screen width
No guideline exists
e: Both Apple HIG and Material recommend ~44–48 dp/pt minimum touch targets and sufficient contrast — improves usability for everyone.
